title: Oscar Romero
hook: an archbishop in El Salvador speaks for the poor and is shot while saying Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, Taizé, one short line sung until it became breathing. Your line was the joy of the gospel. Which line kept repeating in you? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A list of names, read aloud from the pulpit of the cathedral in San Salvador on a Sunday morning. Before it, the archbishop has read the gospel and explained it. Now he reads out the news of the week. People taken from their homes. People found dead by the road. Priests, farmers, students. Across the country, in shops and farmhouses and city apartments, the radio carries his voice. For some of the families listening, it's the one place those names are said out loud. The archbishop's name is Oscar Romero, and when he was chosen, some expected him to keep quiet. Today, how he didn't.

Romero was a careful, bookish priest when he was made archbishop, and some in power were glad of it. Then, soon after, his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit priest who worked among poor farm families, was shot and killed on a country road, along with others traveling with him. Romero went to see the bodies. Those who knew him say something changed in him that night. He began to speak. He spoke for the farmers whose land and lives were taken, for the families of the disappeared, for the poor his country had pushed to the edge. He spoke against killing by any side. He used the pulpit and the radio, and when the church's radio station was bombed, he kept preaching. There's a line in Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction." Dumb there means unable to speak. People came to call Romero the voice of the voiceless. On his last Sunday he spoke straight to the soldiers. Paraphrased: you are our brothers, and no soldier has to obey an order to kill that goes against the law of God. He begged them, in God's name, to stop the repression. The next evening he was saying Mass in the chapel of a hospital where he lived, near cancer patients cared for by sisters. As he finished his sermon and turned toward the altar, a gunman fired through the open chapel door. He fell at the altar. The Catholic Church has since named him a saint, and Christians beyond the Catholic Church remember him too.
screen: `A FRIEND KILLED ON A COUNTRY ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak for the voiceless once. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose story doesn't get told. A worker nobody notices. A patient in a hallway. Someone held somewhere, waiting. A person in a country that doesn't make the news. Hold one of them in mind, and say their situation to yourself plainly, as if you were reading it on the radio. Then think of one place you could say it out loud: a conversation, a letter, a meeting. If you pray, you can pray for them, by name if you know it. The bell holds the time.
Oscar Romero. An archbishop of San Salvador who spoke for the poor and the disappeared, and was shot while saying Mass.

Your line: the voice of the voiceless. Today, pass on one story that isn't being told: tell it to one person, or write it down for someone who can act. This week ran from a Birmingham jail cell to a hospital chapel: a mountaintop, a little light, open windows, old sentences lifted, a song in Taizé. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: The Catholic calendar marks Saint Oscar Romero's feast on the day of his death, and pilgrims visit the hospital chapel in San Salvador where he was killed.
